question: An architect is documenting the permission design for two agent variants built on the Agent SDK: a read-only code review agent and a write-enabled refactoring agent. Which implementation choices should the guidance recommend? (Select all that apply.)
options: A) Include the Agent tool in allowed tools whenever subagents are invoked, since subagent invocations are approved through that tool.
B) Configure the write-enabled agent's permission mode and allowed tools to explicitly include Edit, Write, and Bash as pre-approved actions.
C) Give both agents the same permissive allowed-tools list and rely on the system prompt alone to instruct the read-only agent not to edit files.
D) Grant Bash unrestricted access to the read-only agent so it can inspect file contents via shell commands instead of the Read tool.
E) Configure the read-only agent's allowed tools to include only Read, Glob, and Grep so it cannot modify files even if prompted to.
correct_answers: A) Include the Agent tool in allowed tools whenever subagents are invoked, since subagent invocations are approved through that tool.
B) Configure the write-enabled agent's permission mode and allowed tools to explicitly include Edit, Write, and Bash as pre-approved actions.
E) Configure the read-only agent's allowed tools to include only Read, Glob, and Grep so it cannot modify files even if prompted to.
explanations: Correct. Subagent invocations go through the Agent tool, so it must be included in allowed tools for subagent delegation to be auto-approved rather than blocked.
Correct. Explicitly including Edit, Write, and Bash in the write-enabled agent's allowed tools makes file-changing actions a deliberate, pre-approved part of its configuration.
Incorrect. Relying on the system prompt alone to prevent edits while granting a permissive tool list leaves the read-only guarantee unenforced, since prompts can be overridden or ignored.
Incorrect. Granting unrestricted Bash access to the read-only agent undermines the read-only guarantee, since shell commands can modify files just as Edit or Write would.
Correct. Restricting the read-only agent's allowed tools to Read, Glob, and Grep enforces the read-only guarantee at the permission layer rather than relying on instructions alone.
